H0: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
P1: My own childhood broke many mainstream rules about what children should see and do. I won’t unpack all of it here. I’m grateful that my mother nursed me until I was five, grateful my parents didn’t vaccinate me, and grateful for nearly all of the unusual world they gave me.
CAP1: Me as a child, wearing the pen holder my dad made, ready to write my Final Review 😹
P2: I mention vaccination specifically because it's something I would absolutely need people in a community to agree with me on, if I was going to raise children there. I'm not even considering what would work for everyone, only that there would need to be some common ground among the parents on children's health, enough that they can actually trust one another.
P3: All of this will ultimately be reviewed by the kids, once they're grown, and their review weighs more heavily than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on about their intentions forever, but the kids might have something else to say.

P5: A friend who reviewed this draft grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado where her father was a pastor. She calls her childhood "a treasure and a burden." A treasure because she belonged, and everybody cared for everybody. A burden because of the strict religious life she had no say in.

H1: The Mother Is Primary. The Village Is Real. Neither Replaces the Other.
P7: My view is that moms should raise their own kids, inside a community where the care is really shared. The village can handle meals, supervision, teaching, protection, playing, and a lot of the fathering, but it should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.
P8: A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. It's one outsider's interpretation of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing what she saw, but it's still a powerful picture. She talks about how the babies are carried with them and brought into adult life, how the kids are surrounded by people of several ages and learn by taking part, and how it doesn't fall on one tired parent to be their whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.
P9: Experiments where kids don't sleep and live with their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that they ended the practice of kids sleeping communally for a mix of reasons: developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care and many loving adults in their lives, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.
P10: I'd suggest taking a direct look at what's going on at Tamera's Children's Place instead of caricaturing it. To be honest, my own bias is still toward a system where kids interact with more people, without the parent-child bond being made ideologically inconvenient.
H2: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
P11: Kids also need their own territory, a space to create their own society in, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.
P12: I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's Kinderhaus works from a similar idea. The adults take care of safety on the outside, but the kids still get a world of their own.
P13: I'm making the safeguards explicit, because this could be badly misunderstood otherwise. The adults still have to pay attention to what goes on in a children's territory. Older kids can't quietly lord it over the younger ones there, and secrecy can't pass for independence.
P14: I also think it's a real problem that so many suburban folks treat any warm relationship between a child and an unrelated adult as suspicious. It's good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something's wrong. Fear like that won't actually prevent abuse, but it can destroy that gift.
P15: There are several parts to this protection:
P16: Give children real agency. Kids are allowed to say no, and no grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.
P17: Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it's about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. A surprise isn't a secret, because at the end of a certain date it has to be told. But isolating a kid with secrets isn't allowed.
P18: Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Talk with the kids about the importance of telling the truth, the power of their words, and how what they say will be taken seriously. Don't interrogate them, don't punish them if they're not sure, and don't brush off what they report. A scared or confused kid may tell it wrong and still need protection.
P19: Hear the child even when they point a finger at someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Be clear about the process ahead of time, before anyone's face is attached to it. Do whatever's needed right away to keep everyone safe, then make sure it's investigated competently and fairly, and that nobody's status buys silence.
P20: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 kids in the Island Pond raid, but the state's blanket request was rejected by a court and the kids were returned. Counting on state intervention can fail spectacularly, and enclosing them completely in the community can fail too. Kids need more than one world.
P21: I also looked through my research corpus for good documentation of an actual case, a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, but I couldn't find one that detailed the whole sequence: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. It's possible that there's good documentation but it's private, or that these cases get referred elsewhere. Either way, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest cases on their own. In those cases, the child, the family, and the potential victims all need access to competent help and review, outside the control of the home community.
H3: The Door Must Open Outward at Adulthood
P22: The Amish let their young people make the decision to join the church on their own when they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining. Pop culture makes Rumspringa seem far wilder and more universal than it is, but it's still a big deal that they're baptized as adults, because then belonging is a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.
P23: If the kids never leave, the community has no way of knowing whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, see other ways of living, and disagree with the founders, without treating them as traitors for it.
P24: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
P25a: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. Kids who grow up without ever using money especially need a decent education in how the money world operates, and what to do when they have to deal with it: jobs, rent, contracts, banks, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help.
P25b: They also need a good set of transferable skills and education, good relationships with people outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community). It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, travel expenses, tools or a little money, but even if it can't, it can at least not make things worse by punishing people for leaving, or by holding back knowledge or records a young adult would need to function outside the community. No upbringing can provide perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
P26: It's possible that some of them will split off, either permanently, or into their own communities with different values, rather than wait decades to inherit the original one. And parents may experience that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.
H4: Discuss Child-Rearing Values Before Children Are Caught Between Them
P27: Couples who live together, share the same culture and even the same bed still end up with very different opinions about screens, vaccinations, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. And that's just two people. Now think of twenty adults, all with different childhoods.
P28: Once a kid is already living inside the disagreement, goodwill doesn't answer those questions. The community has to share enough principles about raising kids to hang together, and still leave parents room to decide things for their own kids.
